questions.q: Name the most important tank built in the early years of the fifteenth century at Vijayanagara and state its two primary functions.
questions.a: The Kamalapuram tank, built in the early 15th century, irrigated nearby fields and supplied water to the royal centre via a channel. A wrong answer (e.g., naming the Hiriya canal or a temple tank) reveals confusion between canals and tanks, or between different periods of construction.

questions.q: Why did the rulers of Vijayanagara incorporate agricultural tracts within the fortified area, unlike most medieval cities that only protected granaries?
questions.a: They protected the agricultural belt itself to withstand long sieges that aimed to starve the city; the enclosed fields were irrigated by an elaborate canal system from the Tungabhadra. A wrong answer focusing only on granaries misses the strategic shift from storing grain to protecting standing crops, which required massive fortification walls linking hills.

questions.q: Domingo Paes describes a tank built by Krishnadeva Raya at the mouth of two hills, fed by streams and by pipes from a lake 15 km away. Identify three engineering features of this tank mentioned in his account.
questions.a: The tank had (1) embankments at the mouth of two hills to collect runoff from both sides, (2) pipes running along the hill range bringing water from a distant overflowing lake, and (3) three carved pillars with connecting pipes to draw water for irrigation. A wrong answer that omits the long-distance pipes or the pillars shows inability to extract technical details from a primary source.

questions.q: Compare the water management system of Vijayanagara with that of the Harappan civilization (c. 2600–1900 BCE). Identify two similarities and two differences in their approaches to water storage and distribution.
questions.a: Similarities: both built reservoirs (Harappan Great Bath / Vijayanagara tanks) and used channels for distribution. Differences: Harappans relied on perennial Indus floods and wells; Vijayanagara depended on seasonal Tungabhadra streams and rainwater harvesting in an arid zone. Harappan systems were urban-centric; Vijayanagara’s integrated agriculture within fortifications. A wrong answer that claims both used identical technology ignores the different ecological contexts and political scales.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: “Vijayanagara’s water management was primarily a royal project with little involvement of local communities.” Use evidence from the amara-nayaka system and temple tanks.
questions.a: The statement is inaccurate. The amara-nayakas (military chiefs) maintained irrigation works using part of their revenue, and temple tanks served ordinary town dwellers. Royal projects like the Hiriya canal coexisted with decentralized maintenance. A wrong answer that agrees overlooks the textual evidence that nayakas used revenue for “maintenance of temples and irrigation works” and that wells and temple tanks served common people.

questions.q: Construct a brief argument (4–5 sentences) explaining how the Tungabhadra’s seasonal flow and the region’s aridity shaped the *political* structure of Vijayanagara, referencing the amara-nayaka system and fortification design.
questions.a: A strong argument links the need for large-scale water storage to centralized royal initiative (tanks, canals), the delegation of maintenance to amara-nayakas who controlled local resources, and the decision to enclose farmland within walls to protect the agricultural base during sieges. A weak argument treats water management as purely technical without connecting it to revenue assignment, military organization, or siege warfare.
